newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Clinton envoy visits Central America on trade.
newsitem.headline: Clinton envoy visits Central America on trade.

text.p: Top U.S. government officials visited Guatemala on Wednesday seeking to revive trade with Central America, a region businessmen said the United States had forgotten since the Cold War.

President Bill Clinton's Special Envoy for the Americas, Thomas "Mack" McLarty headed the mission, ahead of Clinton's first visit to the region in May when he is due to meet his Central American counterparts in Costa Rica.
McLarty and top U.S. Commerce Department officials attended a forum in Guatemala City with 100 U.S. firms, who delivered a clear message that the region should not be forgotten.
"We are very glad the Commerce Department is looking at Central America because we felt we were being left behind," Spencer Manners of the American Chamber of Commerce in Costa Rica told reporters.
Manners and other business chiefs said Asian and European leaders have led business delegations to Central America in recent years, while the United States fell behind.
"We have to be extremely careful that the United States does not allow other developed countries to take this market away from us," Manners said.
McLarty agreed the U.S. should not be caught napping.
"This is a natural market for us, but not a captive one," he told reporters.

Trade is at the top of the agenda for Clinton's visit, and the Central American leaders will demand greater access for their exports to U.S. markets. McLarty said he could not predict how Clinton would react to the request.

He drew attention to the major changes in the region, once a battleground for Cold War forces where the United States in the 1980s pumped in billions of dollars to help right-wing governments defeat rebels. All rebel conflicts have now ended.
"Five or 10 years ago it would have been aid, not trade at the top of that agenda," McLarty said.
On Thursday McLarty was due to visit a camp in Guatemala where left-wing rebels who fought the government for 36 years are disarming after signing a peace treaty on Dec. 29.
